title: Human gut microbiota: onset and shaping through life stages and perturbations
abstract: Microbial taxa distribution and density of gut microbiota habitants diverge in different individuals and is modulated by diverse determinants of temporal and spatial variability. Until the moment of birth, the gastrointestinal (GI) tract of a normal fetus is almost sterile. During birth and thereafter, bacteria from mother and surrounding environment colonize the infant's gut by vertical and horizontal transmission. Rapidly after the birth, bacteria start to appear in the feces in a few hours and reach 108–1010 per gram of faeces within a few days. The epithelium at the interface between intestinal microbiota and lymphoid tissue plays a critical role in shaping the mucosal immune response. When commensal/pathogenic bacteria homeostasis is broken up, the perturbation leads to immunological impairment and disease, crucial in “programming early phases” and dysbiosis establishment. Gut imbalance occurring during perinatal and neonatal life can lead to diseases such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), early-inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), respiratory and chronic pulmonary disease, immunological impairment, obesity and metabolic syndrome, hence triggering cardiovascular risks and nutritional impairment further along life stages. Investigation on individuality of gut microbiota onset and modulation requires to speculate on genetic and epigenetic affecting factors. Indeed, relationship between breast feeding, gut microbial taxa, and immune system response appears crucial in early life. However, classical microbiology is underpowered by its inability to provide unbiased representation of gut microbiota. Failure to cultivate in vitro the majority of microbiota taxa hampers a fulfilling description. The advent of high-throughput-omics-based methods, through the holistic view of the “systems biology,” is opening new avenues to the knowledge of the gut ecosystem. In the coming years, the plasticity of the gut microbiota will be even exploited to provide new categories of therapeutics, providing therapeutic modification of the gut microbiota, on the basis of specific microbe-microbe modulation and microbe-host interaction, aiming to correct and improve life style conditions, and medical management of chronic patients such as cystic fibrosis-affected people. Modern microbiology may really concur nowadays in addressing one of the most complicated challenges of the current medicine, the achievement of effective patient-tailored therapies to exactly depict the biology and physiology of the microbiota “organ” of each person. This volume aims to highlight several “frontiers” aspects of gut microbiota studies, through the contribution of 12 articles describing the microbiologist's, the “omics” people point of view, but also the clinician's complementary approaches coming from different expertises and research areas, such as obstetrics, neonatology and hepato-metabolic diseases. The first article, by Pessione (2012), presents a spectacular overview on Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB), ancient microorganisms that, modulating sugar fermentation and decarboxylation/deimination, ensures their survival and colonization in the buffered environments of the GI trait, by a complex molecular cross-talk between LAB and host. LAB proteins, produced in response to gut, promote bacterial adhesion to mucosa and stimulate immune cells. Furthermore, LAB antagonistic relationships with other microorganisms constitute the basis for their anti-infective role. Thus, interesting perspectives for their utilization as antioxidant nutraceutical vectors are hypothesized. The second article, by Rigon et al. (2012) focuses on vertical determinants of gut variability associated to vaginal or cesarean delivery in the mother-child pair, and discuss breast- or formula feeding, also thoroughly discussed in the article by Guaraldi and Salvatori (2012). The two articles are particularly remarkable because they focus, by employing the point of view of the clinician, on the very early phases of gut microbiota programming, still “mysterious” and difficult to be unveiled. A cluster of three outstanding articles addresses, in a fascinating way, the gut “programming” and modification through life stages up to senescence (Kolling et al., 2012; Lagier et al., 2012; Ottman et al., 2012), with special emphasis on gut pathogens occurring during different ages (Kolling et al., 2012), or on data obtained by metagenome, metatranscriptome, and metaproteome integrated approaches (Ottman et al., 2012). Interestingly, Lagier et al. (2012), introduce the novel concept of “culturomics,” a breakthrough in gut microbiota research, with the microbial identification and characterization performed by MALDI-TOF technology. In the review by Kolling et al. (2012), the process of aging is discussed in term of changes due to environmental exposures that subsequently affect the immune system and host-associated microbiota. Within the host's shifting setting, infections by enteric pathogens likely exploit these shifts with resultant initiation of pathogenesis and/or establishment of a mutualistic relationship with the host leading to potential dissemination of the pathogen. There is still much to be learned about how life stages and perturbations shape the gut microbial population, and how these changes influence health and disease and predominant enteric pathogens. Future insights into the interdependency between environment-host-microbe network will be essential for development of novel therapeutic approaches that treat or prevent enteric disease. Understanding the roles of these factors within the host is complementary to external approaches (e.g., sanitation, water treatment) for controlling or eradicating pathogen dissemination. The paper by Berrilli et al. (2012) strengthen the approach undertaken by Kolling et al. (2012), on gut ecosystems and pathogenicity and deal with the inter-play between parasites and microbial gut ecology. The paper has been strongly desired in the e-book Human gut microbiota: onset and shaping through life stages and perturbations, because of the enormous novelty of the topic, still not properly approached by the current literature. Indeed, complex communities, different from bacterial gut ecosystems, including parasites (“parasitome”) and the even less studied fungi (“micetome”), surely co-evolve and interact with the gut microbiome modulating its ecology and physiology, reacting in a different way with and against the host. Indeed, interesting are the parasite immune-modulations at the gut enterocyte level on host immune reaction. On the other site, “omics” technology and their paramount effects on gut microbiota studies have been also deeply described in the articles by Shen et al. (2012) (genomics, metagenomics, and gut modifications), Vernocchi et al. (2012), and Masotti (2012) (gene expression, transcriptomics). Metabolic profiling has a wide potential to understand the complex interactions amongst components of the gut microbiota and to elucidate the relationships (cause/effect) between specific nutritional choices and related shifts in microbiota taxa composition. Particularly, the identification of gut metabolic signatures is extremely challenging, due to its linkage with nutritional choices. In fact, the whole set of metabolites, which can be detected in body fluids and characterizes the metabolic gut-associated phenotypes, can be named “metabotype” (Vernocchi et al., 2012). Dealing with a differential expression of miRNAs in different areas of GI tract can be considered as a function of microbiota composition. In these cases, intestinal microbiota are the “actors.” Conversely, we should also think to miRNAs as “actors” when, under proper conditions, influence the regulation of goblet-cell differentiation. Therefore, an interconnected cycle could be envisaged, as suggested by the Opinion article by Masotti (2012), where miRNAs and gut microbiota are the two main partners. Finally, two remarkable papers by Alisi et al. (2012), and Manco (2012) open new avenues on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), one of the most common causes of chronic liver disease worldwide, and on the gut-brain axis in obesity endophenotypes, respectively. In NAFLD, several observations suggest a potential role of microbiota in NAFLD development, authors suggest that probiotics, for their excellent tolerability, may affect gut microbiota, hence representing promising therapeutic agents to revert NASH-related liver damage. Furthermore, the interesting relationships between gut microbiota and developmental programming of the brain, discussed in the Opinion article by Manco (2012), are providing unpredictable evidence in studies on mental retardation, autism and role of gut dysbiosis through the route to the final outcome of the overt disease. In summary, the articles herein presented, discuss data and matters concerning current investigation and future perspective on gut microbiota studies. In our opinion, further insights will come from interdisciplinary approaches progressively provided by enlarged consortia, including researchers and clinicians, able to exploit high-throughput technological platforms to apply translational workflows in diagnostic pipelines and, finally, in patient care and treatment programs.

title: Complementary roles of glial cells in generating region-specific neuroinflammatory responses and phagocytosis in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Neuroinflammation is associated with Parkinson’s disease: Reactive gliosis and neuroinflammation are hallmarks of Parkinson’s disease (PD), a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons. Neuroinflammation has long been considered a mere consequence of neuronal loss, but whether it promotes PD or is a key player in disease progression remains to be determined. Human leukocyte antigen, also known as major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII), is expressed on all antigen-presenting cells of the immune system including microglia and central nervous system resident macrophages, and interestingly, its expression is increased in post-mortem PD samples (McGeer, 1988; Imamura, 2003). The strongest evidence for a link between the immune system and PD comes from genome-wide association studies, which have identified several polymorphisms in human leukocyte antigen-DR that are associated with an increased risk of idiopathic PD (Harms, 2023). Neuroinflammation is a complex and dynamic process that requires a cross-talk between glial and peripheral immune cells. Understanding these interactions is crucial for developing immunomodulatory interventions that could delay disease progression. Regional states of activation of microglia and astrocytes in the context of dopaminergic degeneration: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system. Their dynamic ramified morphology and their motility allow them to be in a constant state of surveillance. In the adult brain, homeostatic microglia are in contact with neurons, axons, and dendritic spines and participate in synaptic plasticity (Salter and Stevens, 2017). This state can change dramatically when microglial cells are exposed to extracellular stimuli. Brain regions with specific neuronal activity, different neuron:glia ratios, and morphological and transcriptomic microglial heterogeneity would drive a context-dependent switch of these cells (Paolicelli, 2022). The dynamic nature of these states needs to be addressed in the context of neurodegeneration. Subcortical structures such as the ventral midbrain, which contains dopaminergic cell bodies, and the striatum, which contains GABAergic medium spiny neurons receiving dopaminergic afferents, are poorly characterized. Dopamine plays a key role in the control of basal ganglia function, and impairment of the nigrostriatal pathway is implicated in the motor symptomatology of PD. Analysis of glial activity in the midbrain and striatum would provide new clues to understanding the regional heterogeneity of the brain and new opportunities for therapeutic intervention in PD. The transcriptomic profile of midbrain and striatal CD11b+ cells shows that pathways involved in immune function and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) complexes are overexpressed in the midbrain, while those involved in synaptic function are underrepresented (Abellanas, 2019). Compared to the striatal cells, midbrain microglia (CD11b+CD45low) show a high state of immune alert with increased expression of TLR4, major histocompatibility complex class I (MHCI), MHCII, CD80, and CD86 and unique cell subsets, one MHCII+ with antigen-presenting properties and another TLR4+. As a result, higher levels of CD4 and CD8 T cell infiltration are detected in this region (Figure 1A). Systemic administration of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced a classical pro-inflammatory response with the production of tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), interleukin (IL)1β, and IL6 in both regions and a specific increase of IL10 and transforming growth factor β in the midbrain. The production of these anti-inflammatory cytokines was accompanied by a loss of MHCII expression, a decrease in CD4 T cell infiltration in the midbrain, and an increase in regulatory T cells (Figure 1B). Morphological changes in microglia indicated an altered activation state, but did not correlate with their inflammatory profile. We concluded that the high basal immune alert state of the midbrain elicits immunosuppressive responses when exposed to an inflammatory stimulus (Abellanas, 2019).Figure 1: Glial activation states in the ventral midbrain and striatum in response to various stimuli.Schematic representation of the inflammatory and phagocytic phenotype of microglia and astrocytes, and the infiltration of peripheral immune cells in: (A) homeostasis (Abellanas, 2019), (B) systemic LPS administration (Abellanas, 2019), (C) αSyn overexpression (Basurco, 2023), (D) subacute and (E) chronic MPTP injection (Ayerra, 2024). Created with BioRender.com. αSyn: α-Synuclein; cMPTP: chronic MPTP mouse model; IL10: interleukin 10; IL1β: interleukin 1β; IL6: interleukin 6; LPS: lipopolysaccharide; MHCI: major histocompatibility complex class I; MHCII: major histocompatibility complex class II; sMPTP: subacute 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine mouse model; TGFβ: transforming growth factor β; TLR4: toll-like receptor 4; TNFα: tumor necrosis factor α; Treg: regulatory T cells.Neuroinflammatory microglia can induce a neurotoxic polarization of astrocytes by secreting TNFα, IL1α, and the complement factor C1q (Liddelow, 2017). Astrocytes, provide support to neurons by controlling ion and nutrient balance, participate in synaptic transmission, and are part of the blood–brain barrier (Han, 2021). The loss of homeostatic functions of glial cells and the acquisition of new activities may have an impact on disease pathogenesis. Therefore, we investigated about the functional state of microglia and astrocytes during the active phase of nigrostriatal pathway degeneration using experimental models of PD. In the α-synuclein (αSyn) overexpression mouse model, an adeno-associated virus was injected into the substantia nigra pars compacta to overexpress αSyn or the control protein mCherry. In these mice, we distinguished between an early stage with mild motor symptoms (2 weeks) and a late stage with severe motor impairment, neurodegeneration, and weight loss (4 weeks). To understand the early neuroinflammatory events that occur during dopaminergic dysfunction, we focused on the activation state of microglia and astrocytes at 2 weeks, hypothesizing that their functionality would differ between the striatum and the midbrain (Basurco, 2023). CD11b+ cells in the midbrain showed a phagocytic and an anti-inflammatory profile that was distinct from microglial signatures described in other neurodegenerative diseases (Keren-Shaul, 2017). In this region, astrocytes were the main pro-inflammatory players with a neurotoxic phenotype (Liddelow, 2017) and increased expression of transcripts associated with TNF, interferon γ and IL6 pathways. At the same time, a pro-inflammatory phenotype close to that of disease-associated microglia (Keren-Shaul, 2017) was detected in striatal CD11b+, which was not accompanied by morphological changes or by variation in the activation state of astrocytes. Iba1+ cells were actively involved in the clearance of cellular debris in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The relative increase in CD11b+CD45high cells detected by flow cytometry and in Iba1+ cells not expressing Tmem119, suggests that monocyte/macrophage infiltration in this area may play a relevant role in the early stages of neurodegeneration or when microglial cells are overwhelmed by the extent of neuronal damage. The mild loss of striatal dopaminergic terminals did not attract CD11b+CD45high and did not allow the detection of phagocytic activity (Figure 1C; Basurco, 2023). To determine whether glial activation states are generated by αSyn overexpression or by nigrostriatal degeneration, we used the 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) mouse model. Dopaminergic neuronal death was induced by two intoxication regimens, subacute (sMPTP) and chronic (cMPTP) (Ayerra, 2024). The sMPTP induced an inflammatory response with a different contribution from each cell type. In the striatum, the pro-inflammatory phenotype of CD11b+ cells was counteracted by the anti-inflammatory astrocytic profile. In the midbrain, the roles were reversed, with CD11b+ cells exhibiting an anti-inflammatory profile and astrocytes being pro-inflammatory. The balance of the inflammatory responses resulted in reduced CD4 and CD8 T cell infiltration in both regions (Figure 1D). In contrast, cMPTP exposure resulted in a mild and prolonged neuronal loss that induced a pro-inflammatory response and increased CD4 T cell infiltration in the midbrain (Figure 1E). The phagocytic activity of glial cells was different in the two MPTP administration regimens. In addition, to eliminate the “time of analysis” factor, a new set of mice with the cMPTP administration regimen was generated and termed early cMPTP (ecMPTP). These animals were processed at the same time as the sMPTP mice and showed a milder motor impairment, but no nigrostriatal degeneration. At the onset of the neurodegenerative process (sMPTP and ecMPTP), microglia and astrocytes cooperated in removing striatal dopaminergic terminals. Over time (cMPTP), only microglia maintained the phagocytic activity. In the ventral midbrain, the lack of activation of a phagocytic program in microglia at the early stages of neurodegeneration (sMPTP and ecMPTP) was compensated by astrocytes, which were the main phagocytic mediators in this region. An increased number of infiltrating CD11b+CD45high and CD4 T cells was detected exclusively in ecMPTP mice suggesting that these cells may play a relevant role in the prodromal stages of the disease. As the dopaminergic lesion becomes chronic (cMPTP), only phagocytic microglia were detected in the midbrain. Overall, these results suggest that the inflammatory status and phagocytic activity of glial cells depend on the region, the intensity of neuronal damage, and the stage of degeneration. Morphological changes do not reflect the inflammatory state of glial cells. In the short term, midbrain CD11b+ cells generate an anti-inflammatory response in the presence of an intense stimulus such as LPS, αSyn, or MPTP, which becomes pro-inflammatory after chronicity of the lesion. In contrast, striatal CD11b+ cells always display a pro-inflammatory profile. The phagocytic activity of CD11b+ cells depends on the region and the stage of the degenerative process. Concluding remarks: Neuroinflammation is at the intersection of the major risk factors for PD, genes, environment, and aging. To target neuroinflammation as an intervention strategy, it is necessary to understand the dynamics of this response in the striatum and the midbrain and its impact on neuronal viability. The midbrain has unique properties in the generation of neuroinflammatory responses, with a high basal immune alert state generating a short-term anti-inflammatory response, in contrast to the classical pro-inflammatory response generated in the striatum. The anti-inflammatory microglial profile in the midbrain may represent an early event in neurodegeneration, and whether it protects or exacerbates neuronal death remains to be investigated. Interestingly, the activation state of microglia correlates with T cell infiltration, suggesting that these cells, rather than astrocytes, would drive immune extravasation in this region. Dopaminergic degeneration in PD is progressive, whereas in the experimental models is triggered simultaneously. Comparison of human and mouse glial cell phenotypes shows that the cMPTP mice better recapitulate the pro-inflammatory and phagocytic state of midbrain microglia sequenced from PD patients with advanced disease (Smajic, 2022; Ayerra, 2024). Early events in this model (ecMPTP) may help to understand prodromal glial activation states and their relationship to degeneration. Considering that glial cells stablish dynamic inflammatory and phagocytic phenotypes in the time course of the neurodegenerative process, it would be necessary to define therapeutic windows. The cooperativity between microglia and astrocytes suggests that therapeutic strategies should target specific glial activation states rather than a cell population.
